directAnswer: Pope Sergius IV, born Peter in Rome, reigned from 1009 to 1012. He was bishop of Albano before his election, served under the influence of the Crescentii, and was remembered for his care for the poor.

sections.h2: Peter 'Bucca Porci' and the Name Sergius
paras: Sergius was born in Rome, by some accounts the son of a shoemaker, and his own baptismal name was Peter. He was nicknamed Bucca Porci, often translated as 'pig's snout.' Some later tradition holds that he changed his name to avoid reigning as Peter II out of reverence for the apostle. Before his election he was bishop of Albano, near Rome, and some lists describe him as a Benedictine.

Sergius became pope on 31 July 1009, likely with the approval of John Crescentius. Despite that dependence, he is credited with relieving poverty in Rome during a period of famine, and his epitaph praises his generosity to the poor. He also granted privileges to monasteries and maintained cordial relations with Henry II of Germany.

In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. A letter attributed to Sergius calls on Christians to free the holy places, but most historians doubt its authenticity and believe it may have been composed later, around the time of the First Crusade. Sergius died on 12 May 1012 and was buried in St. John Lateran.

keyFacts: Born Peter in Rome; nicknamed Bucca Porci
Remembered for aiding the poor during famine
A crusading letter in his name is of doubtful authenticity

faqs.question: What does 'Bucca Porci' mean?
faqs.answer: It is a Latin nickname usually translated as 'pig's snout.' It was attached to Sergius IV, whose original name was Peter.

faqs.question: Did Sergius IV call for a crusade?
faqs.answer: A letter attributed to him urges the liberation of the Holy Sepulchre after its destruction in 1009, but historians widely regard it as a later composition.
